damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Mill House / Spinner's End) — Snape's defence against Bellatrix's accusations is entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 26–46 establish a long, forensic cross-examination in which Snape systematically dismantles every one of Bellatrix's accusations — why he wasn't there when Voldemort fell, why he didn't search for him, why he blocked Quirrell, why he returned late after the Dark Mark burned, why Potter is still alive — with cold, precise, confident rhetoric. This extended passage is the primary characterisation of Snape as a master double-agent: supremely intelligent, in total control of the room, and operating on multiple levels simultaneously.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 compresses the entire Spinner's End meeting to a brief exchange. Snape says only that he has 'played his part well' and has 'deceived one of the greatest wizards of all time.' Bellatrix's long list of accusations, and Snape's methodical, confident rebuttal of each, is completely absent. The audience sees none of his reasoning, none of his controlled dominance over Bellatrix, and none of the specific intelligence about his long game.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Spinner's End chapter is the single most important scene for establishing Snape as a brilliant, calculating, multi-layered figure rather than simply a menacing teacher. Removing it strips his later reveal of almost all its groundwork. The film gives him one vague boast instead of a sustained demonstration of wit and nerve. This directly damages the audience's ability to understand or believe in Snape's arc when it pays off at the end of the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Mill House) — Snape's motivation for the Unbreakable Vow is simplified to anger at Bellatrix's taunting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 58–63: In the book, Snape agrees to the Unbreakable Vow after a moment of visible blank, unreadable consideration — his expression described as 'blank, unreadable.' The decision is entirely internal and opaque, which is consistent with his double-agent complexity. He does not react to Bellatrix's insults as a trigger; his agreement is calm and deliberate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 3, Snape's eyes flash with anger at Bellatrix's taunts ('Bloody coward... he'll slither back into his hole') and he turns to her with anger visible before ordering her to take out her wand. The film frames his agreement as a hot-blooded response to provocation, implying he acts to prove a point to Bellatrix rather than from cold strategic choice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Snape chooses deliberately and inscrutably; the film's Snape appears stung into action. This is a small but meaningful shift that reduces his agency and makes him seem reactive rather than in control, slightly undermining the portrait of a man who never loses his composure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage — Riddle's Room, Pensieve) — Tom Riddle's explanation for keeping stolen objects is rewritten
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 254–255: When Dumbledore asks what the stolen objects are and why Riddle took them, Riddle says nothing that reveals warmth or need for connection. Dumbledore tells him to return them to their owners 'with your apologies.' Riddle does not look 'remotely abashed' and watches Dumbledore 'coldly and appraisingly.' The subsequent analysis (Book Scene 281) makes clear these are trophies of cruelty, souvenirs of power over victims — the 'magpie-like tendency' Dumbledore identifies as a key to understanding the Horcruxes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 7, when Dumbledore asks 'Why did you want these things, Tom?', Riddle answers: 'I like having things that belonged to other people. It makes me feel... close to them.' This is an invented line not present in the book corpus. It reframes trophy-collecting as a manifestation of loneliness and longing for connection rather than predatory dominance and the desire to possess trophies of victimisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This rewrite is directly damaging because Dumbledore's analysis of Voldemort's magpie-like trophy-collecting is the foundation for understanding why he chose the specific objects he turned into Horcruxes. The film's substitution — loneliness rather than predatory domination — makes Voldemort more sympathetic and obscures the link between his childhood cruelty and his later choices. It also misrepresents the psychology of a character Dumbledore explicitly describes as incapable of love or genuine connection.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Mrs. Cole's gin-drinking scene and her detailed account of Riddle's history are cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 207–219: Mrs. Cole gives Dumbledore a detailed account over gin — the girl who arrived and died, Riddle's naming, the rabbit hanging from the rafters, Amy Benson and Dennis Bishop being 'never quite right' after the cave visit. Dumbledore uses gin and charm to extract this; the scene establishes both the method (flattery and social intelligence) and the content (a catalogue of childhood sadism escalating in seriousness). Her final comment — 'I don't think many people will be sorry to see the back of him' — is significant characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 cuts directly to the corridor and Mrs. Cole mentions only that Tom is 'odd' and there have been 'nasty things' with other children, giving no specific examples. There is no gin, no extended account, no detail about the rabbit or the cave children. The film moves immediately to Riddle's room.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The specific incidents Mrs. Cole describes in the book — particularly the cave visit — are directly relevant to the cave sequence later in the film. Their absence means the cave's emotional and narrative weight (Riddle terrorising children here as a boy) is only stated by Dumbledore in a single line rather than shown to have been established by witness testimony. It also removes texture from young Riddle's portrait of escalating, calculated cruelty.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Riddle's demand that Dumbledore prove himself and his commanding tone are softened
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 227–232: Young Riddle says 'I don't believe you' with 'ringing force,' speaks the words 'Tell the truth!' as 'a command,' and later says 'Prove it' 'at once, in the same commanding tone.' When Dumbledore says he won't force him to come, Riddle sneers 'I'd like to see them try.' The book stresses that Riddle already behaves like someone accustomed to exerting power over others.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7 has Riddle say 'I don't believe you. I hear Mrs. Cole talking...' in a measured, contained way, and 'Prove it' as a flat statement. The confrontational commands ('Tell the truth!', the sneer about seeing them try) are absent. Riddle is more watchful and still than imperious and commanding.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's young Riddle already displays the instinct to dominate and issue commands — he has 'given it many times before.' This is a deliberate early marker of Voldemort's core personality. The film's Riddle is more passively menacing (staring, stillness, spiders) which is atmospheric but loses the specific quality Dumbledore later identifies: Riddle's contempt for authority and his compulsion to be obeyed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Riddle does not go alone to Diagon Alley; the exchange about his father's identity is cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 257–271: Riddle says bluntly 'I didn't have any money' (without thanks for the money bag), insists 'I don't need you. I'm used to doing things for myself,' and then, just as they are about to part, 'as though it burst from him in spite of himself,' asks 'Was my father a wizard?' Dumbledore notes he had 'withheld mention of this strangest power until that moment, determined to impress' with the Parseltongue revelation. These beats show self-sufficiency, suppressed need, and the nascent obsession with paternal identity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7 ends with Riddle revealing Parseltongue and Dumbledore departing, but the entire exchange about going alone to Diagon Alley and Riddle's question about his father is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The question about his father — erupting involuntarily despite Riddle's careful self-control — is one of the few moments in the books where Voldemort's suppressed human wound is visible. Dumbledore's later analysis of Riddle's obsession with his parentage (Book Scenes 321–322) is partially unmoored without this seed. The self-sufficiency detail also reinforces the 'operates alone' trait Dumbledore flags as key to understanding the Horcrux strategy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 / Scene 17 (Slughorn Horcrux memory, both corrupted and true versions) — The true memory omits Riddle's visible greed and the specific question about seven
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 538–559: The true memory (obtained by Harry) shows Riddle's 'hunger' becoming 'apparent' and his expression becoming 'greedy, he could no longer hide his longing.' When Riddle asks about splitting the soul more than once and specifically proposes 'isn't seven the most powerfully magical number,' his face at the end is described as showing 'wild happiness... the sort of happiness that did not enhance his handsome features, but made them, somehow, less human.' Slughorn is shown genuinely regretting the conversation and 'gazing at Riddle as though he had never seen him plainly before.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 17 includes the key content (the seven question, Slughorn's horror) but Riddle's physical tells of naked greed and the description of his face becoming 'less human' with happiness are not conveyed — the film presents him as controlled throughout, only turning away to look in a mirror with a hint of red in his eyes. Slughorn's moment of truly seeing Riddle for the first time is not dramatised.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of the true memory is important not only for the information content but for what it reveals about Riddle's mask slipping — a rare moment of unguarded hunger. The film's version preserves the plot but loses the characterisation: the sense that even at sixteen, Riddle was barely containing something monstrous behind his polished facade.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Dumbledore's Office after Horcrux memory) — Entire analytical framework about Voldemort's past, multiple Horcruxes, and specific objects is drastically compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 561–632: After seeing the true memory, Dumbledore delivers an extended analysis covering: the confirmed existence of multiple Horcruxes; that Riddle probably made six plus the seventh in his body; the locket and cup as likely candidates; the diary already destroyed; the ring already destroyed; Nagini as a probable Horcrux; the prophecy's true meaning (Voldemort created his own enemy); love as power; Harry's freedom of choice. This is a major expository and thematic scene spanning dozens of pages.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 18 compresses this to: seven Horcruxes confirmed; the diary and ring already identified; brief mention that they 'can be anything'; a flash of images (ring, cup, snake, derelict house) when Harry touches the ring; and Dumbledore saying he may have found another and asks Harry to come with him. The specific identifications of likely objects, the discussion of Nagini, the analysis of why Voldemort preferred Horcruxes to the Sorcerer's Stone, and the extended discussion of love and prophecy are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This compression significantly damages the audience's understanding of the Horcrux quest that will drive the entire next film. The book's scene is where Harry (and the audience) receives the intellectual and emotional framework for everything that follows: why these specific objects, how many, what has already been done, and what Harry's real power is. The film substitutes a brief visual montage and leaves most of the strategic and thematic content unspoken. The discussion of love as Harry's defining power — one of the saga's central themes — is entirely absent from the film corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 — Dumbledore's reaction to learning Snape passed on the prophecy is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 636–642: Harry confronts Dumbledore with the revelation that Snape overheard the prophecy and reported it to Voldemort, leading directly to the deaths of his parents. Dumbledore's face whitens. Harry rages. Dumbledore defends Snape, saying Snape did not know which boy would be targeted, and that his remorse 'is the greatest regret of his life and the reason he returned.' Harry demands to know how Dumbledore can be sure, and Dumbledore says 'I trust Severus Snape completely.' This is a pivotal scene for Snape's arc and Dumbledore's relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This confrontation does not appear in the film corpus at all. The revelation about Snape and the prophecy, and Dumbledore's defence of him, are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is crucial for three intersecting arcs: Snape's hidden motivation (remorse over Lily's death), Dumbledore's trust in Snape (and the reason behind it), and Harry's justified fury. Removing it means audiences in the next film will lack the emotional and narrative groundwork for Snape's full revelation. It also removes a key beat in the Dumbledore-Harry relationship where Harry's anger is legitimate and Dumbledore's defence of Snape is costly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Cave) — Dumbledore's commentary on Voldemort's psychology during the cave sequence is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 648–671: Throughout the cave sequence, Dumbledore offers a running analysis of Voldemort's thinking — why the boat is sized for one wizard's power, why Voldemort didn't worry about a child's magic registering, why the island's poison won't immediately kill its victim (Voldemort wants information first), why Voldemort fears death and darkness while claiming superiority. Each observation illuminates Voldemort's psychology and his specific blind spots.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 19 presents the cave sequence as primarily physical and atmospheric. Dumbledore speaks about the blood toll at the entrance and briefly about the place 'knowing magic,' but the sustained psychological commentary about Voldemort's design choices, his fear of death, and his underestimation of youth is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the cave as a teaching moment — Dumbledore demonstrates his method of reading Voldemort's mind through the physical evidence of his defences. This models for Harry (and the audience) the kind of thinking needed to defeat Voldemort. Its absence means the cave is primarily spectacle rather than the penultimate lesson in Dumbledore's curriculum for Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 20 (Astronomy Tower) — Dumbledore's disarming and the tower confrontation with Malfoy is changed in a way that alters Dumbledore's agency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus does not contain the tower scene in the excerpt provided, but Book Scene 678 references the tower events (Malfoy's boasts, Snape's vow, 'he'll slither back'). The book establishes that Dumbledore was immobilised by a Petrificus curse before being disarmed — he did not willingly allow Malfoy to Expelliarmus him. Harry, hidden and immobilised by Dumbledore's prior spell, could not act.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 20 shows Dumbledore deliberately and slowly drawing his wand ('without intent') as if to offer it to Malfoy, effectively inviting the Expelliarmus. Dumbledore appears to choose to be disarmed as a tactical or compassionate gesture toward Malfoy. Harry, hiding below, is not shown to be under any binding spell — he chooses to stay hidden on Dumbledore's instruction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's version transforms Dumbledore from a man caught off-guard while already weakened into a figure making a deliberate, almost Christ-like surrender. While this is a valid interpretive choice, it removes Harry's anguish at being physically prevented from acting — in the book, Harry is bound by Dumbledore's spell and cannot intervene even if he wanted to. The film's Harry simply obeys an instruction, which is less dramatically devastating and removes the specific guilt of paralysis that the book creates.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Grounds chase) — Snape reveals he is the Half-Blood Prince during the chase
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 683–685: During the chase, Snape deflects Harry's spells and orders him not to use Occlumency against him ('Blocked again and again and again until you learn to keep your mouth shut and your mind closed, Potter!'). The revelation of the Half-Blood Prince identity does not occur during the chase in the book — it is discovered separately.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 21 has Snape reveal 'Yes. It's me. I'm the Half-Blood Prince' during the chase itself, as a parting taunt. This is a significant restructuring of when and how this revelation lands.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moving the Half-Blood Prince revelation into the heat of the chase transforms it from a discovery Harry makes in grief and reflection into a villain's parting taunt. It reduces the quiet horror of realising the mentor figure of the annotated textbook was the same person who just killed Dumbledore, and converts a moment of complex irony into a melodramatic exit line. The emotional and thematic weight of the revelation is diminished.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Great Hall feast) — Dumbledore's speech about Voldemort is vague and brief; the deeper context established in the book is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 144: Dumbledore's feast speech in the book directly names Voldemort, emphasises the danger, and is described as making the 'silence seem to tauten and strain.' It is substantive and direct. The book corpus also establishes (Scenes 68–69) that Dumbledore had already spoken directly to the Dursleys about the open state of war and Harry's danger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 has Dumbledore give a speech that mentions Tom Riddle's student days and warns that 'dark forces attempt to penetrate this castle,' but the central warning is diffuse and ends with the odd, deflating 'their greatest weapon remains... you' / 'Just something to keep in mind. Now, off to bed. Pip pip!' Ron comments 'That was cheerful' — the film itself flags it as an anticlimactic non-speech.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's Dumbledore frequently undercuts gravity with deflating humour ('Pip pip') in a way that slightly softens his authority and the seriousness of the threat. In the book, the feast speech carries genuine weight. This is a recurring pattern in the film's Dumbledore characterisation across this instalment — consistent with the broader criticism of the adaptation — but the corpus evidence for this specific scene supports a modest impact weight.

main_damage_causes: The near-total removal of Snape's extended self-defence at Spinner's End strips the double-agent characterisation of its most important dramatic evidence, damaging audience investment in and comprehension of his arc across the remaining saga.

The compression of Dumbledore's post-Horcrux-memory analysis removes the thematic and strategic framework — love as Harry's true power, the specific Horcrux candidates, the prophecy's real meaning — that the book uses to prepare the audience intellectually and emotionally for the final two films.

The rewriting of young Tom Riddle's psychology at the orphanage (stolen objects as loneliness rather than predatory trophy-collecting) misrepresents the foundation of Voldemort's character and partially severs the explanatory link between his childhood and his choice of Horcrux objects.
